deep.reconstruction:
Context. The page continues sheet 'Litt. F' of the 1805 drafts. The previous page reduced a Piazzi observation of 1802 May 23 (Palermo) with Gauss's 'VII. Elemente'. The time count runs from 1802 Jan 0. The three times on this page, 25.689, 84.518 and 143.304 d, fall on Jan 25, Mar 25 and May 23, 1802. Pallas was only found on Mar 28, 1802, so the planet is almost certainly Ceres. This identification is my inference. The page is the numerical core of a first hypothesis in Gauss's determination of an orbit from three geocentric places, the procedure later codified in Theoria Motus (1809), Book II, Sect. 1. The next page carries the 'Zweite Hypothese' with the same quantities corrected.

(1) Geocentric data (upper left). Three longitudes are listed: A = 182°49'51.82", A' = 174°27'42.36", A'' = 171°7'30.58". Beside them are differences and corrections. Below come logarithmic tables for each pair of places: log tan, log cos, log sin, and cos of the latitude-type angles. Two columns are typical, e.g. tg 0.7057998 / 2.1171251 and cos 9.9319382 / 9.9817964. Heliocentric-earth data follow, e.g. log R and the triangle quantities 9.9933838, 0.0056917 and log sin of small differences. All are 7-place logarithms in Gauss's usual convention: characteristic +10, n = negative.

(2) Intervals ('Die Zeiten'), with θ = kτ:
- t = 25.6893565, 84.5184803, 143.3036134.
- τ'' = t' - t = 58.8291238 and τ = t'' - t' = 58.7851331.
- τ' = t'' - t is written 117.6141569; the exact value is 117.6142569.
- With log k = 8.2355814 (Gauss's constant), log kτ = 8.2355814 + 1.7692675 = 0.0048489, log kτ'' = 8.2355814 + 1.7695924 = 0.0051738, and log kτ' = 0.3060413.
- These serve as first approximations f = 0.0048489 and f'' = 0.0051738. In the first hypothesis the ratios of the triangles n/n', n''/n' are taken in proportion to the time intervals.

(3) The poles of the great circles. From the previous page come the poles P, P', P'' of the great circles through pairs of geocentric places, and the quantities p, q, q''.
- Gauss forms log(1/sin P') = 10 - 9.4389978 = 0.5610022.
- He forms log(sin P''/sin P) = 9.9716150 - 9.9059363 = 0.0656787.
- An auxiliary angle x is introduced with log tan x = 8.8742321, log sin x = 8.8730187, log cos x = 9.9987866, giving x = 4°16'51.61".
- Then 19°42'20.47" - 4°16'51.61" = 15°25'28.86" (p - x).
- A first chain (log 8.1877179 ...) is struck through, together with an abandoned trial value x = 13°56'52.91". It is redone as follows: 8.1877995 + 9.9806516 = 8.1684511, then + 9.9737913 = 8.1422424, and so on to 9.2942190. Subtracting cos x gives 9.2954324. Then 9.2954324 + 9.9763205 + 0.5610022 = 9.8327551, which is labelled k sin p' and agrees with 9.8327548 in the left column.
- The relation is summarised as 8.4466475·f + 9.9078310·f'' = f'·sin(u - 4°16'51.61")/sin u'. This is a linear relation between the curtate distances or areas of the type used in Gauss's elimination. The coefficients are logs.

(4) Lower left. Combining f, f'' with the coefficients:
- 8.4466475 + 0.0048489 = 8.4514964 and 9.9078310 + 0.0051738 = 9.9130048.
- Their antilog-sum leads to 9.9277577, and then to 9.5271402 (k sin p') and on to 9.4548979 and 8.7509043.
- Angle bookkeeping:
  - 3°4'9.90" + 4°16'51.61" = 7°21'1.51".
  - + 0°9'39.56" gives 7°30'41.07". A first value 7°33'20.10" is cancelled.
  - Then 7°30'41.07" - 6°7'0.83" = 1°23'40.24".
  - 7°30'41.07" - 4°16'51.61" = 3°13'49.46".
  - 7°30'41.07" - 4°20'51.46" = 3°9'49.61".
  - 6°7'0.83" and 4°20'51.46" are the arcs from the previous page.
- Column 0.0100227, 8.5814206, 1.4286021 ... M = 0.9832590 ... 9.1163580 yields log r' = 0.4107862 (labelled f'). It also yields 0.7039936, with 0.0048489 and 0.0051738 repeated.

(5) Centre ('Nach der 2ten Methode', 'Nach der 3 Methode'). The radii vectors are computed by two independent routes. Pairs of columns:
- log values 0.6991447 / 0.6988198, 0.4669385 / 0.5326172 (= log sin-ratios of the previous page), 8.3862565 / 8.7418630, ...
- log tan 0.7057998 / 2.1171251.
- These give log r = 0.4074678 then 0.4074962, and log r' = 0.4163308, later (0.4163456).
- On the right the computation is repeated by the 2nd and 3rd methods. Both give log r' = 0.4163495 and 0.4163504. Agreement to 1 unit in the 7th place is the check.

(6) Heliocentric longitudes and arcs (lower right).
- 21°34'14.48" - 26'15.04" (= q'' of previous page) = 21°7'59.44".
- From the longitude-type angles 8°1'25.44" and 21°7'59.49":
  - half-sum 14°34'42.465"
  - half-difference 6°33'17.025"
  - 86°21'52.95" and 81°49'0.13" are the further angles.
- Log chains: 9.4008929 + 9.9957797 = 9.3966726; 9.0574844 + 9.1421881 = 8.1996725; 9.3966726 - 9.9991253 = 9.3975473; ... These give the heliocentric arcs:
  - half of the total arc 14°27'50.99", total arc 28°55'41.79"
  - 'Zweiter Bogen' 14°18'29.70"
  - 'Erster Bogen' 14°37'14.18"
- The partial arcs sum to 28°55'43.88", about 2" more than the total. This residual is the defect of the first hypothesis, and the next page reduces it.

(7) Bottom. A sum check of logs (9933838 + 5161841 + 4771997 + ...) compares geocentric log distances: 0.22828 ('Dist. 1'), 0.27757 ('inv. 2'), and 0.27776 ('vera', i.e. from the VII elements). The note '21°7'56.60", Error 3"' compares the computed heliocentric longitude with that of the elements.

Summary. A complete numerical test of Gauss's three-observation orbit method, on 1802 observations of Ceres against his own 7th elements, carried out in 1805 while he was refining the methods published in Theoria Motus.
errors: The interval t''-t is written 117.6141569. The exact difference 143.3036134-25.6893565 is 117.6142569, a slip of 1 in the 7th decimal (or a misreading). The log used, 2.0704599, matches the correct value 2.0704600, so nothing downstream is affected.
The value 9.9972173 is labelled 'cos 6°', but log cos 6° = 9.9976143. The label is probably misread (some other angle near 6.5° is meant), or the entry belongs to a different quantity.

The first (struck-out) column in the centre-top is internally inconsistent: 9.2941131 - 9.9987866 is not 9.2954595. Gauss abandoned it, together with the trial x = 13°56'52.91", and recomputed correctly in the next column, where 9.2942190 - 9.9987866 = 9.2954324 and the sum gives 9.8327551.

The partial heliocentric arcs 14°18'29.70" + 14°37'14.18" = 28°55'43.88" exceed the total arc 28°55'41.79" by about 2". This is the expected residual of a first hypothesis, not a blunder. It is corrected in the 'Zweite Hypothese' on the next page.

results.what: Orbit determination from three geocentric observations: hypotheses on the ratios of the triangles (first approximated by the ratios of the intervals kτ), solved for the curtate distances via the poles of the great circles, then iterated
results.modern_name: Gauss's method of initial orbit determination

results.what: Computing the radius vector by two independent routes ('2te' and '3te Methode') as a consistency check (0.4163495 vs 0.4163504)
results.modern_name: Alternative formulae for the heliocentric distance in Gauss's method
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss, Theoria Motus Book II

results.what: Comparison of computed heliocentric arcs and geocentric distances with values from the 'VII. Elemente' (error about 3")
results.modern_name: Testing an orbit method against known elements

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine working computations of Gauss's own, well-documented orbit-determination method, applied to 1802 Ceres observations. They are of interest as evidence of how he tested variants of the method in 1805 before Theoria Motus, but contain nothing not already credited to him.

checkable.asserts: ≈ 2.09 s residual between partial arcs and total arc (first hypothesis)

transcription_corrections: In the boxed angle column '3.9.49,68' is most likely '3.9.49,61' (7°30'41.07" - 4°20'51.46").
'117,6141569' as written; the correct difference is 117.6142569.
The label 'Bodrolt' beside 123°45'39"69 is uncertain; it may be a node or longitude designation.
The struck-out entries ('x 13.56.52.91', 'tg x 8.8742221', '7.33.20.10') are cancelled trial values, not results.
